proof_summary: For a proper odd prime divisor \(q\mid n\), setting \(t=\operatorname{ord}_q(2)\) and using the valuation of \(2^{tj}-1\) matches every \(q\)-factor in \((n-1)!\) to a numerator factor, with the omitted multiple \(n\) supplying one extra factor of \(q\); hence \(q\mid a(n-1)\), while the remaining composite case \(n=2^r\) is excluded by the exact value \(v_2(a(2^r-1))=r-1\). Once \(n=p\) is prime, if \(2\) had order below \(p-1\), the factor \(2^{\operatorname{ord}_p(2)}-1\) would make \(p\mid a(p-1)\); in every case the assumed divisibility would then force an odd prime (or an insufficient power of \(2\)) to divide the accompanying power of \(2\), a contradiction.
